content: Pain is the most frequently encountered symptom in emergency medical settings. However, the management of acute pain in pediatric patients remains suboptimal. Intranasal drug delivery has emerged as a promising alternative to intravenous administration, offering faster drug delivery while avoiding the additional distress associated with inserting an intravenous cannula in children. The objective of this review was to identify and evaluate all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials that compared intranasal fentanyl (INF) with other analgesic interventions in children experiencing acute pain. The outcomes assessed included pain score reduction, adverse events, patient tolerability, the need for rescue analgesia, patient and parental satisfaction, and mortality. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, LILACS, CAB Abstracts, ISI Web of Science, BIOSIS Previews, CNKI, ISRCTN, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, covering studies published from 1995 to January 2014. The inclusion criteria were RCTs comparing INF with any other pharmacological or non-pharmacological intervention for children under 18 years of age experiencing acute pain. Two independent reviewers assessed the relevance of each study and evaluated the methodological quality using the Cochrane Collaboration's risk of bias tool. Effect sizes were measured using mean difference (MD), odds ratio (OR), and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Three studies, involving a total of 313 participants, met the inclusion criteria. One study compared INF with intramuscular morphine (IMM), another compared INF with intravenous morphine (IVM), and the third compared standard concentration INF (SINF) with high concentration INF (HINF). All three studies demonstrated a reduction in pain scores following the administration of INF. When comparing INF with IMM, a greater reduction in pain scores was observed at 10 minutes post-administration in the INF group (pain score: 1/5) compared to the IMM group (pain score: 2/5), with a statistically significant P value of 0.014. However, no statistically significant differences in pain scores were observed at other time points. When INF was compared with IVM, both treatments resulted in a statistically significant reduction in pain scores up to 20 minutes post-administration. Beyond this time point, no further reduction in pain scores was noted for either treatment. When comparing SINF with HINF, both groups demonstrated a statistically and clinically significant reduction in pain scores over the study period, with a median decrease of 40 mm and a P value of 0.000. No adverse events, such as opioid toxicity or death, were reported in any of the studies following INF administration. One study reported better patient tolerance to INF compared to IMM, with this difference achieving statistical significance. However, some participants reported a bad taste and vomiting associated with INF use. The overall risk of bias in the included studies was considered low. The authors concluded that intranasal fentanyl may be an effective analgesic for managing moderate to severe acute pain in children, with minimal associated distress. However, the review does not provide definitive evidence regarding whether INF is superior, non-inferior, or equivalent to intramuscular or intravenous morphine. Limitations of the review include the small number of eligible studies (three), the absence of studies involving children under three years of age, the lack of studies addressing pain from medical causes (e.g., abdominal pain due to appendicitis), and the fact that all included studies were conducted in Australia. As a result, the findings may not be generalizable to other healthcare settings, to children younger than three years, or to those experiencing pain from medical conditions.
